limitations.statement: Every reported success rate / accuracy in the evidence package is a single run with no variance, standard deviation, seed count, or significance test.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: Comparisons phrased as 'above'/'below' a baseline (e.g. 26.0% vs. 27.3%) describe raw point differences only; none is established as statistically distinguishable from noise.

limitations.statement: Two pairs of numbers in the source tables conflict for the same reported quantity: SWE-Bench Lite gpt-4o-mini (6.3% vs. 7.0%) and GPQA-diamond expert-human accuracy (81.3% vs. 81.2%).
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: Neither conflicting pair is adjudicated by this evidence package; both values are reported side by side rather than one being asserted as correct.
limitations.resolution: Unresolved; flagged as CONFLICTING_EVIDENCE. No human reviewer is available in this run, so both values are disclosed rather than averaged or arbitrarily chosen (accepted_risk, recorded in state.json).

limitations.statement: The HumanEvalFix comparison between OpenHands (0-shot) and SWE-Agent (1-shot) uses different amounts of task demonstration.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: The gap between 79.3% and 87.7% partly reflects the shot-count difference and cannot be attributed to agent design alone.

limitations.statement: The evidence package does not state whether AgentBench and MINT baseline agents were tuned or run with a compute/prompt budget comparable to OpenHands.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: Head-to-head comparisons on AgentBench OS and MINT should be read as reported outcomes under unstated relative budgets, not as budget-controlled comparisons.

limitations.statement: WebArena and MiniWoB++ baselines that outperform OpenHands (Auto Eval & Refine, AutoWebGLM, CC-NET, Workflow Guided Exploration) use different training paradigms: reward models, reflexion loops, or dedicated reinforcement learning / behavior cloning on the benchmark itself.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: OpenHands trails these systems partly because they are purpose-built and trained for the benchmark, whereas OpenHands is a general zero-shot prompted agent; the comparison bounds the generalist claim rather than contradicting it outright.

limitations.statement: The GAIA L1 validation subset used for evaluation has only 53 instances.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: A 32.1% vs. 13.2% gap on 53 instances is a coarse estimate; small-sample noise is not quantified.

limitations.statement: On ProofWriter, OpenHands is given the logical forms produced by Logic-LM rather than parsing the problem itself.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: The near-parity with Logic-LM (78.8% vs. 79.6%) is not evidence that OpenHands solves the semantic-parsing step; it is evidence about reasoning given parsed input.

limitations.statement: The source material's own description of cross-domain performance as 'competitive' has no stated numeric threshold, and OpenHands is below baseline on at least four of the evaluated benchmarks (WebArena, MiniWoB++, MINT code, Entity Deduction Arena).
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: The generalist-performance interpretation is read here as a qualitative pattern across categories, not as a claim that OpenHands leads every, or even most, individual benchmarks.

limitations.statement: Community metrics (contributions, contributors, GitHub stars) are self-reported and time-varying, not measured under any fixed evaluation protocol.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: These numbers describe project adoption at one point in time, not a scientific result, and should not be read as a proxy for a benchmark score.
